name: Mahali
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

sources.citation: Language Division, ORGI. Linguistic Survey of India - West Bengal (Part I) (2016), - Bihar (2020), - Orissa (2021).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Full texts a full-text search for stress/accent Mahali/Mahili/Mahle/Mahli: no Mahali chapter in any of the three (Bihar has one mention in a list of tribes). Not copied to the maha1291 folder.

sources.citation: Ghosh, Arun. 2008. Santali. In Gregory D. S. Anderson (ed.), The Munda Languages, 11-98. London: Routledge.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Santali (not Mahali): p. 11 'Words are predominantly dissyllabic with stress on the second syllable in dissyllabic and multisyllabic words, and on the root vowel if it is monosyllabic'; pp. 29-30 (2.5 Suprasegmental phenomena) 'Santali has no phonemic tones or registers.. Stress is always on the second syllable of a word unless it is monosyllabic, irrespective of whether it is an open or a closed syllable'; p. 31 'In words with more than one syllable the second syllable gets the stress.' Mahali appears only in the classification map, no dialect discussion in the preview.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.1 languoid page for Mahali (maha1291); ISO 639-3 code page for mjx; Wikipedia 'Mahali language' (redirect to Santali language).
sources.note: Glottolog lists no descriptive references (only Prasad 1976 and Kim et al. 2010 for subclassification, Eberhard et al. 2025 for endangerment); ISO page: individual living language 'Mahali'; Wikipedia treats Mahali (Mahili) as a Santali dialect and gives only the Santali stress line (Ghosh 2008: second syllable).

sources.citation: Language Division, Office of the Registrar General, India. 2023 [PDF dated 2021]. Linguistic Survey of India - Jharkhand. Chapter 'Mahili' by P. Edward Vedamanickam, pp. 827-869 (survey data: Singhbhum district, Gidini block, Dec 2000-Jan 2001).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Section 2 Phonology (pp. 831-840) covers segmental phonemes, '2.1.2 Supra segmental phonemes' (p. 832: 'Though length and nasalization are not phonemic in this mother tongue, yet it appears in Mahili mother tongue'), distribution, clusters and syllable structure (p. 840); no stress, accent, tone or intonation statement anywhere in the chapter (a full-text search for stress/accent the extracted text: only 'stress' in the grammatical sense, p. 851). Intro states 'Mahili mother tongue spoken in Bihar is not different from the Santali language' (p. 830).

sources.citation: Kim, Seung, Amy Kim, Sayed Ahmad & Mridul Sangma. 2010. The Santali Cluster in Bangladesh: A Sociolinguistic Survey. SIL Electronic Survey Report 2010-006. Dallas: SIL International. 223 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing. Sociolinguistic survey with IPA wordlists from three Mahali villages (Abirpara, Matindor, Pachondor) and a Mahali text; lexical similarity with Santali above 74%, 'only the Mahali.. can possibly be called a dialect of Santali' (p. 21-22). No stress or phonology description.

sources.citation: Grierson, George A. (ed.). 1906. Linguistic Survey of India, Vol. IV: Munda and Dravidian Languages. Calcutta: Office of the Superintendent of Government Printing. 'Mahle' section pp. 74-76; Santali 'Accent' paragraph p. 38.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.harvard_location: Widener Library, call number 3254.1 F; Linguistics Library, call number CoPh 5.40; a Harvard library, call number Ud 0010
sources.note: Mahle section: 'They speak a dialect of Santali'; 'Pronunciation' notes (vowel quality, diphthongs, n/l for ny, r for R) but no accent statement for Mahle. The Santali section (p. 38) says: 'Accent.-In words of two syllables the accent usually rests on the first. Thus serma, year. The final syllable is, however, accented when it ends in a semi-consonant, when the last syllable is long and the first short, when the word ends in n, and when it is a reduplicated or reflexive monosyllabic base.. There are many exceptions to the general rule, but we have no detailed information about the matter.'…
